slides.title: A clear chart
lines: Turn a small table into a chart.
Check its labels and values.
Explain what the chart shows.
slides.cue: Point, write, type or speak quietly to an adult.
slides.notes: Model first. Use fictional practice points, not real prices or personal data. Offer private answers and pink paper. No required reading aloud, cold calling or forced sharing. Each pupil uses their own file.

slides.title: Check the starting values
lines: Watch the adult check one value.
These are points, not packs or money.
A chart is only as useful as its data.
slides.notes: Retrieve Week 4: a displayed total needs checking. Model Task B4=20 from the supplied data card. The fresh task reproduces the accepted Week 4 final totals: 20, 10, 8. A learner may compare their earlier file, but use this fresh Task sheet for shared cell addresses.

slides.title: What do we want to compare?
lines: We want to compare three items.
A column chart makes heights easy to compare.
Use the item names and total points.
slides.cue: Choose the two needed columns in private.
slides.notes: Model identifying categories and numbers. Explain that a column chart has upright bars; a horizontal bar chart is also valid if the learner explains it. A line chart could suggest an order through time that these categories do not have. Do not require a tour of other chart types.
answers: Use item names and their total points, not the whole total.

slides.title: Choose the chart range
lines: Watch the Model sheet first.
Select A3:B6, including the headings.
Leave the whole total in row 7 out.
Insert a simple column chart.
slides.cue: Check that there are three columns.
slides.notes: The Model sheet has a completed chart for rehearsal. Delete its chart in a disposable copy to demonstrate from scratch. Use A3:B6: paper 6, card 6, fasteners 4. Row 7 totals 16; it is not a fourth item. Keep the pupil Task sheet unchanged.

slides.title: Make the chart clear
lines: Give the chart a useful title.
Show each item name and the unit points.
Start the number scale at 0.
Use equal steps and a flat chart.
slides.cue: Match one column height to its table value.
slides.notes: Model title Model kit points, item labels, vertical axis Total points and horizontal axis Item. Use a zero baseline and equal steps of 2 to 10. No 3-D effects. Check both equal values reach 6 and fasteners reach 4. Ask each pupil privately to match one value before moving on.

slides.title: Read a chart with care
lines: Read the title, labels and scale.
Name the unit when you give a value.
Equal heights mean equal values here.
slides.cue: Point to the scale and its starting value.
slides.notes: Use the words page. Model: paper and card both use 6 points; fasteners use 4. A bar height of 6 does not mean 6 packs. The chart compares points for different item types, not how many packs are needed.

slides.title: Test a linked chart
lines: Predict what will happen to one column.
On Model, change B6 from 4 to 10.
Check the chart against the table.
Restore B6 to 4 after the test.
slides.cue: Tell the adult which column changed and why.
slides.notes: Model the prediction first, then let each pupil choose or state the changed column privately. Fasteners rise from 4 to 10 points and become highest; paper and card stay 6. The total becomes 22 but is not plotted. If the chart stays fixed, inspect its data range and whether it is a pasted picture. Restore B6=4.

slides.title: Is the total another item?
lines: The table has three items and a total.
This chart shows four columns.
Should the total be a fourth item?
slides.cue: Choose yes or no privately, with a reason.
slides.notes: Hinge: no. The total combines the same three items and is not an extra category. If either pupil accepts it, point to the rows and reselect A3:B6. Use up to 90 seconds here. Parallel hinge: a column reaches 20; can we call it 20 packs? No, the axis unit is points.
answers: No. The total already includes all three items.
Keep the three item rows; leave the whole total out.

slides.title: Chart my activity kit
lines: Use the Task sheet and data card.
Make and label a chart of the three items.
Change B4 from 20 to 12 and check it.
Explain a comparison, then save.
slides.notes: Slides 9-13 share twelve minutes. Task deliberately has data but no chart. Each pupil creates and checks their own chart. One device: two six-minute turns while the other plans in their book. Protect the selection, labels, update and reopen checks.
example: A chart linked to the cells

slides.title: Supported
lines: Open Task. Check the three values on the data card.
Select A3:B6, including headings but not the total.
Insert a simple column chart. Use three columns.
Add a title and labels. Check the scale starts at 0.
Predict, then change B4 from 20 to 12. Check the chart.
slides.cue: Use one step at a time; make your own choices.
slides.notes: Point to A3:B6 and fade help. Let the learner choose the range and labels before any exact adult typing. Record that access support. If time is short, offer the title frame Activity kit ... and preserve the change test.

slides.title: Independent
lines: Check the Task data and choose the chart range.
Make a column chart to compare the three items.
Add a clear title and labels that show points.
Check the scale starts at 0 with equal steps.
Change B4 from 20 to 12 and explain what changes.
slides.cue: Check the range, labels and scale before saving.
slides.notes: Accept a clear horizontal bar chart with a zero baseline and correct units. A colour change alone is not an improvement. Inspect source ranges and all three plotted values; the correct picture alone does not prove that the pupil created a linked chart.

slides.title: Aspire
lines: Complete the Independent task first.
Compare paper and card points before and after the change.
Explain why a scale starting above 0 can mislead.
State one thing this chart cannot tell us.
Keep B4 at 12 and check all three columns.
slides.cue: Use two values to support each comparison.
slides.notes: Initially paper exceeds card by 10 points: 20 minus 10. After the change the gap is 2: 12 minus 10. Starting a bar scale above zero exaggerates lengths. The chart does not show preferences, reasons for the kit, real prices or pack counts. Keep the fair scale and B4=12.

slides.title: My chart evidence
lines: My chart compares ...
After the change, ... uses ... points.
This is ... points more than ...
I checked the chart by ...
slides.cue: Show your chart and saved file privately.
slides.notes: Record title, range, units, zero baseline, before/after change and a valid comparison. Example after change: paper uses 12 points, 2 more than card at 10. Give one next step, wait for a pupil response and acknowledge it privately. A paper chart is planning evidence, not proof of a digital linked chart.

slides.title: Read a new chart
lines: Which item uses the most points?
How many more than paper packs?
Could this chart tell us the favourite item?
slides.cue: Give a private answer, then reopen your file.
slides.notes: Two minutes transfer, three minutes save/reopen and private feedback. Card uses 8 points, 4 more than paper at 4. No preference data is shown, so favourite item is unknown. Do not infer digital chart creation from a correct spoken or written answer. Week 6 is accessible presentation; Week 7 is assessing.
answers: Card packs: 8 points, 4 more than paper packs.
The chart does not show favourite items.

pupil_pages.title: Knowledge organiser
sections: The aim
I can make a clear chart and use its data to explain a comparison.
Choose a chart
A column chart compares separate items using upright bars. A horizontal bar chart can also work.
Choose the data
Use the item names and their points. Do not plot the whole total as another item.
Make it clear
Use a clear title and labels. Show the unit points. Start the number scale at 0 with equal steps. Avoid 3-D effects.
Check a change
Change one source value and check the matching column. The other columns should stay the same.

plan_pages.title: Teacher and cover plan
sections: Lesson

A clear chart | Tuesday 1 December 2026 | Tuesday P6 | 40 minutes
LAUNCH pair. Year A. Formative; Week 7 is assessing.
Aim
I can make a clear chart and use its data to explain a comparison.
Theme
Identity & Belonging: explain a fictional shared activity kit clearly while keeping each learner responsible for their own work.
Careers
Office and stock roles use charts to explain resource needs. A clear chart and a checked comparison can show a digital skill in an application.
Prepare

Open the fourteen-slide lesson or HTML page. Open Spreadsheet_Practice.xlsx in a spreadsheet. Task has data and no chart; Model has a completed chart. Save a fresh copy for each learner. Print the data card, chosen route and evidence prompts; offer pink paper. Use books, pens and up to two devices.
Participation

Model first. Use private responses, no cold calling and no required reading aloud. Offer pointing, typing, book work or quiet conversation. Read privately on request. Keep pupil answers off the shared display.
Success

I chose the three items and their points.
I used a clear title, labels and a scale from zero.
I checked a change, explained a comparison and reopened my file.

plan_pages.title: Lesson sequence
sections: 0 to 3 minutes  Arrival
Slides 1-2. Check Task points against the data card. Retrieve the Week 4 check habit.
3 to 7  Starter
Slide 3. Choose item names and points to compare.
7 to 10  Model selection
Slide 4. On Model select A3:B6 and create a column chart. Exclude row 7.
10 to 13  Model clarity
Slide 5. Add title, labels and points. Use zero and equal steps. Match a column to a cell.
13 to 15  Words
Slide 6. Teach category, axis and scale using the chart.
15 to 20  Together
Slide 7. Predict Model B6=10, test the update, then restore B6=4.
20 to 23  Hinge
Slide 8. Should the whole total be a fourth item? Re-model if needed; parallel check tests units.
23 to 35  Task
Slides 9-13. Create a Task chart, label, change B4 to 12, compare and save. One device: six minutes each.
35 to 40  Exit
Slide 14. Read a fresh chart, reopen saved work and respond to one next step.

plan_pages.title: Modelling and adaptations
sections: Model data and chart

Model points are 6, 6 and 4; whole total 16. Use A3:B6. The supplied completed chart is a rehearsal and fallback; delete it in a disposable copy for live modelling. Title: Model kit points. Item labels; vertical axis Total points; horizontal axis Item. Scale 0 to 10 in steps of 2.
Change demonstration

Predict B6 changing from 4 to 10. The fastener column rises to 10; paper and card remain 6. Whole total becomes 22 but is not plotted. Restore B6 to 4. A chart must be linked to its cells, not a pasted picture.
Cognition and learning
Chunk selection, chart insertion and labels into separate steps. Point to one item and its value. Fade from a complete model to a range prompt, then an independent check. Keep the data visible.
Communication and EAL
Use the word page and frame: ... points is ... more than ... . Allow planning in any language. Accept pointing to two bars before a written or quiet spoken comparison.
SEMH and access

Use predictable stages and quiet thinking time. No learner comparison or surprise public question. Offer a brief pause within stage time. Provide pink paper, zoom, uncluttered view and exact adult typing if needed; record that support.
Misconceptions
The total is another item: it combines the same data, so exclude it. A taller bar means more packs: the axis shows points. A decorative chart is clear: inspect units, values and scale first.

plan_pages.title: Evidence and next steps
sections: Core evidence

Observe range A3:B6, three plotted values, title, item labels, unit, zero baseline and equal intervals. Check the B4 change, a comparison with two values and a reopened saved file. Distinguish pupil choices from adult typing.
Task answers

Initially 20, 10 and 8 points; whole total 38. After B4=12 the chart is 12, 10 and 8; total 30. Paper remains highest. Paper exceeds card by 10 before the change and 2 after. Keep B4=12. The total row is not plotted.
Saving and turn-taking

Use ICT_Practice/W05_Charts. Save as Chart_A_v1 or Chart_B_v1 with the workbook extension. One device: two six-minute turns, each in their own file. The other pupil plans in their book. Aspire keeps v1 and saves v2.
Feedback

Give one success and one NS. Record VF, WS or I accurately. The pupil responds in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode or private mode. Use R only after the response and an adult audience have both happened.
Paper fallback

Draw and label a chart in the book from the same data. This shows planning and interpretation. Mark digital chart creation, linked update and saving not yet observed; complete these when a device is available.
Progression
Secure: clear linked chart and accurate comparison. Developing: wrong range, unclear units or untested update. Revisit one step. Week 6 makes an accessible presentation. Week 7 is assessing.

staff_pages.title: Staff answers
sections: Data choice
Use item names and total points: A3:B6 on either sheet. The headings belong in the selection; row 7 does not. A column or horizontal bar chart is suitable for this comparison.
Model checks
Paper 6, card 6, fasteners 4. Total 16. When Model B6 changes to 10, only fasteners rise; total 22. Restore B6=4. The total is never plotted.
Task checks
Initial chart: 20, 10, 8. Paper is highest and exceeds card by 10. After Task B4=12: 12, 10, 8. Paper still leads; the paper-card gap is 2. Total changes from 38 to 30. Keep Task B4=12.
Hinge and parallel check
The total is not a fourth item; it adds the same three items. Re-select A3:B6. A value of 20 is 20 points, not 20 packs. Check the axis unit before making a claim.
Transfer exit
Card uses 8 points; paper and fasteners each use 4. Card uses 4 more points than paper. Favourite item is unknown: no preferences are shown.
Valid comparison
After the change, paper uses 12 points, which is 2 more than card at 10. Accept other accurate comparisons that name items, values and units.

staff_pages.title: Checks and feedback
sections: Aspire
Paper-card gap falls from 10 to 2 points. Starting the column scale above zero can exaggerate apparent differences. The chart cannot tell us preferences, reasons, prices or pack counts.
Chart inspection

Check the plotted categories and source ranges. Check that item labels match values. Keep equal intervals and zero baseline. A single series needs no legend if title and labels are clear. Accept readable horizontal bars with the same checks.
If the chart does not update

Check it is a native chart linked to Task A3:B6, not an image. Inspect the data selection and the changed cell. Refresh or recalculate if needed. Record any application issue instead of claiming the update was observed.
If the chart is confusing

Remove the total category, 3-D effect or extra series. Restore the item labels and points unit. Give the chart space so labels fit. Check the source table before changing data to match an expected picture.
One next step
Choose one: fix the data range; label the unit; restore a zero baseline; test the update; use two values in a comparison. Wait for a private pupil response and acknowledge it.
Evidence boundary
An adult-made chart, a supplied model or a correct oral answer does not prove independent digital chart creation. Record exactly what the learner selected, entered, explained and checked.

staff_pages.title: Support adult brief
sections: Before
Offer white or pink paper and a private response mode. Prepare fresh copies. Model is the adult example; Task is the pupil workspace.
Model
Point to selected cells, chart columns and labels. Show that row 7 is outside the chart range. Give processing time and check one matched value.
Together
Use the prompt ladder: point to instruction; ask a short question; rephrase; offer a scaffold or choice; model the first step only, then return the task.
Independent
Prompt the next check without supplying the whole solution. Use exact typing if agreed and record it. One device: change turns at six minutes while the other pupil plans in their book.
Record
Keep individual evidence of selection, chart creation, labels, scale, update and reopen. Distinguish access support, reasoning prompts and adult correction.
Close
Give one next step privately. Wait for a response and acknowledge it. Mark digital work not yet observed if only a paper chart was made.

sequence_pages.title: Sequence and evidence guide
sections: The discrete ICT sequence

Year A, Autumn 2. Week 1 files and personal information; Week 2 a structured document; Week 3 evaluating sources; Week 4 spreadsheet formulas; Week 5 charts; Week 6 accessible presentation; Week 7 independent task with a paragraph frame, assessing.
This lesson
Tuesday 1 December 2026, P6. Week commencing 30 November. One 40-minute lesson for the LAUNCH pair. Public and school teaching content is identical and generic.
Evidence to retain

An individual saved workbook with a linked chart; a checked source range, labels, scale and changed value; a comparison; actual support and reopen observation. Do not infer success from the supplied model.
Print and access

Use the data card, one route and evidence prompts. Offer pink PDFs or ordinary PDFs on pink stock. Plan and respond in books or a private file. No required reading aloud, cold calling or public answer.
Next lesson
Accessible presentation on Tuesday 8 December 2026. Keep the checked chart available as possible content. Week 7 is the assessing lesson.
